report:
**Conclusion: yes—among people at high risk from substantial current or past smoking, regular *low-dose* CT (LDCT) screening reduces the chance of dying from lung cancer.** Your proposed “no” is therefore not supported by the best randomized-trial evidence.

The pivotal U.S. National Lung Screening Trial randomly assigned high-risk participants to annual LDCT or chest X-ray. There were 356 lung-cancer deaths with LDCT versus 443 with X-ray—a **20% relative reduction**. This is mortality evidence, not merely evidence that CT finds more early cancers.  
https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4817217/

The independent Dutch-Belgian NELSON randomized trial compared repeated LDCT with no screening. It likewise found significantly lower lung-cancer mortality; at 10 years, the rate ratio in men was **0.76** (about a 24% reduction).  
https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa1911793

This benefit applies to carefully selected high-risk people and organized screening programs—not to everybody, and not to diagnostic standard-dose CT. The USPSTF concludes with moderate certainty that annual LDCT has a moderate net benefit for people at high risk, but emphasizes real downsides: false positives, follow-up imaging or invasive procedures, overdiagnosis (finding cancers that would not have harmed the person), incidental findings, distress, and small radiation risk.  
https://www.uspreventiveservicestaskforce.org/uspstf/recommendation/lung-cancer-screening  
https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33687468

Screening does not prevent cancer and does not replace quitting smoking; it improves the odds of surviving lung cancer by detecting some treatable cancers earlier. Individual eligibility, health status, willingness to undergo follow-up/treatment, and local program quality matter.
